app: 24. ADHD Organizer- Llama Life - Focus timer, habits, routines
text:
Amazing app for my adhd and a much happier life! . I struggle with time management, time blindness, prioritising, planning, overwhelm etc etc. I tried llama life free for two weeks and found it so helpful. TBH I was reluctant to pay because I was not sure if I would stick to it and I don’t have much cash so I tried to find a free alternative. 

I tried loads of the mainstream ones recommended- but they were all so complex and overwhelming. 

Llama life looks deceiving simple. But it works amazingly for me. I had a little system in my house of index cards in a box. My friend suggested it to me because I get so overwhelmed with lists. 

Each index card had a task on it and I’d put them in a box standing up with  little headers- urgent, medium, long term. A list totally overwhelms me but I found that having each task on a separate card, I could more easily choose what was important and shuffle around my order. And put some back in the box. 

I also hate tech of any kind so not keen on apps but came across a podcast with llama life creator which inspired me to then search for the app. 

It’s like my little cards plus it’s colourful and pretty to look at. The confetti after each task helps boost me a little. I can shuffle my cards around into different orders. I can prioritise by moving some onto the ‘ not now’ list so I can just focus on what I’m doing today in the next few hours.  The time I’ve estimated for each task is then translated into real time at the top of the task so I know when I finish a task and whether the MANY tasks I’m  planning will fit into my day.

I nearly always run over on my estimations of time. I love that you can choose to let time roll over so you can see how long u actually spent. And the little summary page is brilliant at the end of the day. I take a screenshot at the end of my eve and then clear the completed tasks for the next day. With time ( if I get round to it) I’d like to look at my screenshots of data and see if I can get better at judging time. 

Another handy thing is if I’ve planned e.g. put washing out and then something distracts me while doing this task and the timer is ticking away, I can add it to my task description so I can still track my activity and time taken. 

I honestly never write reviews and I never thought I’d love an app on my phone but after two weeks without it, I really wanted to buy it because it feels so helpful for keeping me focused. I am so happy to support fellow adhd creators for the time and clarity of this app. I thank them from the bottom of my never ending bottomless to-do list! And heart 💙👍

text:
If I could give it 10 stars, I would . I’ve had DUE for longer than I can remember, and I’ve always loved it. It’s simple, it’s easy, and—unlike so many other apps—it doesn’t cost a small fortune. It’s an affordable annual purchase (not an endless subscription), and it does exactly what it promises, in the cleanest and most straightforward way possible.
I never write app reviews because the best apps tend to fade into the background—you use them, rely on them, and stop thinking about them. But this app deserves recognition.
Earlier this year, I was diagnosed with ADHD, and everything suddenly clicked. I realized that DUE has always worked so well for me because of how frictionless it is. When something pops into my head that I need to remember, I can instantly throw it into DUE. No complexity. No setup. No mental overhead.
What truly sets this app apart is the reminder system. I don’t use calendars, task lists, or to‑do apps anymore because things get buried, endlessly snoozed, or turned into meaningless deadlines. DUE is different. If you don’t check something off, it just keeps reminding you—gently but persistently—without you having to manage or reset anything. That “nagging” feature works quietly in the background, doing exactly what it’s supposed to do. It’s simple, effective, and honestly kind of genius.
Now, DUE is where everything goes—anything I need to remember, no matter how big or small. And the funny thing is, I appreciate this app more now than I ever did when I downloaded it over five years ago. It continues to improve, continues to get better, and I genuinely don’t know what I would do without it.
Huge appreciation to the people behind this app for keeping it affordable, simple, and incredibly effective. This is the first app review I’ve ever submitted—and it’s long overdue.

You can leave this open, even with your phone on silent, and still hear the time ticking away, which is enough auditory stimulation for me to focus on what I’m doing. app: 10. Finch - Self-Care Pet - Daily Journal & Habit Tracker
text:
Hands down the best app for so many things . I describe this app to my friends as a self care tamagotchi and recommend it to everyone I know who has ADHD, Autism, anxiety, depression, or who simply wants a fun, highly customizable, gamified habit tracker and journaling app. Seriously. Finch does it all! 

I love being able to set my own routines, set reminders, customize the icon that goes with it, habit stack within a goal, etc. And the fact that doing things that help me to take care of myself and my home also earns gems that I can spend to dress up my little bird or decorate her house? Amazing! It makes me want to accomplish more each day. 

I’ve always struggled with breath work and meditation. Finch has made both of those much easier for me. I also love the focus timer for when I’m working on a project that I’m not really interested in but need to work on nonetheless. 

My advice for those new to Finch: start small with a couple of key tasks throughout the day. Reward yourself for what you are already doing too. As you integrate new habits, add a few more. If a habit is one you consistently avoid, pause and come back to it later when you might be better prepared to start again. Don’t fill your day with tasks you hate. That can make you want to avoid the app altogether. Some goals just aren’t realistic for where you are at in your life right now and that’s okay! 

Good luck! Enjoy! 

And if you wonder if premium is worth it? It really really is! Plus, they send you an email ONE MONTH before they charge for your renewal. This is a great app by great developers who simply want to make life better for people who struggle. And there are zero ads.

app: 24. Fabulous - Daily Habit Tracker - Morning Routines & ADHD Help
text:
Fabulous Meilleur investissement de 2025 . Fabulous est basé sur la science! Les neurosciences 🧠
Fabulous m’aide au quotidien depuis 2 mois. C’est la première fois de ma vie, en 36 ans d’existence, que j’ai une routine! C’est magique 🪄

Je pensais que c’était impossible pour moi de réussir cet exploit si insignifiant pour les adultes neurotypiques.

Pour être exact, je n’ai pas une routine: j’ai 3 routines!

Fabulous me suggère une routine pour le matin, le midi et le soir.

J’ai fait plusieurs essais avant de trouver l’ordre qui me convient pour les étapes de mes 3 routines. J’ai maintenant un rythme que je suis capable de tenir tous les jours.

Jamais je n’aurais pas être #thatGirl. La femme qui est capable de tenir un journal quotidien.

Comme femme TDAH je sais à quel point tenir un journal m’aide à avoir les idées claires.

Comme femme bipolaire, je sais à quel point un journal d’humeur est utile pour [essayer] de prévoir les manies et les dépressions.

J’ai découvert que, comme la plupart des gens, le concept de « strikes » me motive. 

Les personnes TDAH ont un manque chronique de dopamine. C’est mon cas.

En 2 mois je n’ai réussi aucune strike pour la tâche [Fil dentaire] 🦷. Je lâche pas!

Si ça fonctionne pour le yoga, les étirements quotidiens et la course 🏃🏾‍♀️ j’ai confiance que je vais réussir pour le Fil dentaire au moins 3 journées d’affilée.

Vraiment Fabulous est mon meilleur investissement de 2025. Peut-être même à vie… qui sait 🤔

Ce qui fait le succès de Fabulous à mes yeux c’est l’esthétisme de l’app 🎨

Le design UX/UI est abouti.
J’ai trouvé un seul bug mineur qui ne m’a jamais empêché d’utiliser l’app.

Les citations sur fond de décor de la nature ne sont pas ketaines. Les citations de personnes inspirantes sont toujours pertinentes.

Fréquemment je prends une capture d’écran de l’infographie ou de la citation du jour.

Fabulous propose régulièrement de partager à nos proches. C’est du marketing, certes, mais selon moi un bon marketing.

J’ai personnellement utilisé la fonction Partager pour inviter un ami dans mon défi [1 minute d’étirements].

J’ai aussi partagé le défi [Travail avec un partenaire] avec une amie qui est travailleuse autonome. 

Fabulous m’aide à être une meilleure personne. Pour moi-même. Pour mes proches. Et pour mes collègues et mes boss!

Fabulous à été créé pour les personnes TDAH. Comme femme autiste Fabulous m’aide au quotidien également.

Je souffre de ARFID. Fabulous m’aide à manger sur une base régulière. 

Les questions prompts comme [Quels est mon aliment sain préféré?] m’aide à identifier mes « safe foods ».

Très utile pour préparer mon premier RDV avec le nutritionniste. 

Merci aux créateur.ices de Fabulous 🙏🏼 
Grâce à vous, ma vie va bien. 😌 Bien mieux.

app: 5. Routine Planner, Habit Tracker - Daily Time Management for ADHD
text: Completely worth it. Amazing app for ADHD brains . This app is one of the most useful tools I've ever used to combat procrastination and other ADHD related difficulties. I love how flexible it is to be able to adapt to what I specifically need. I especially love that I can skip a part of my routine and it still marks the entire routine as completed (you can see in the details what you skipped). This is a big deal for me because it removes the feeling of missing something and the guilt that could entail. People often say "just start" but it feels like every part of a bigger task needs that decision to start. With this app, I just need to decide to start the routine, the rest is decided. It's gotten me to be more consistent with my workouts (I just added 15 minutes of yoga to the end of my morning routine) and with my studies. But I use it for anything I do regularly that involves more than two sequential actions. The big thing is, YOU need to decide start. The app can remind you, but only you have the power to take that action. But once you've done that, the app (and your past self who created the routine) removes the decision fatigue from the rest of that routine. I seriously and wholeheartedly recommend this app!

text:
Genuinely life-changing! . I have ADHD (primarily inattentive type) and it used to be so tough to get through my morning & night routines efficiently and without forgetting something or being worried I did. This app helps me so much.

I’ve even started using it to plan out entire days or afternoons, if I have a lot of school work or a to-do list to work through. I’m taking classes and working online right now & since there’s so little natural structure in my days, it’s really tough to keep myself on track sometimes. When I’m on autopilot it’s easy to somehow get through a day without doing anything I wanted or needed to do. No matter how detailed a plan I make or how hard I try to do things in a certain order or at a certain time, I just won’t do it. But this app adds just enough extra structure / incentive to change that. Maybe it’s because once I start a “routine,” I can’t see the whole list at once, so I’m less tempted to get distracted or jump around. But now when I plan my day in the morning or the night before, I actually feel like I can stick to it (at least to some extent lol).

I’ve tried so many different apps for productivity, habit tracking, staying organized, etc. over the years, and I kind of gave up on finding one that really worked for me, but then I started looking again and found this. It’s genuinely been so helpful, as evidenced by the fact that I felt compelled to actually review an app for the first time in my life lol.

app: 65. TickTick-To Do List & Calendar
text: Since joining their very affordable monthly subscription, I've found TickTick to be an indispensable part in my daily routine, and it's actually helping me be more productive even though I'm a pretty begrudging procrastinator. First off, the widgets. God, I love the widgets! The first thing I see after unlocking my phone is A) a list of all the stuff I need to be doing on that given day; and B) a cute visual checklist of daily habits that I need to also make time for. This was what I found was missing back when I used the ToDoIst app, was a simple means of having both habits and to-dos living in the same shared ecosystem. I suppose there are technically more dedicated habit apps with deeper tracking features, but what's here is perfectly functional, and easily integrates into your regular 'inbox'/'today' lists. The widgets update dynamically, right along with the full-screen app, and also with the PC and web integrations. This was a "must-have" feature, because I've tried other productivity apps where there is lag time between inputs on the widget, and seeing them "refreshed" into existence several minutes later in the app itself. TickTick makes everything instant, to the point that a TickTick notification 'pings' on my phone at the precise moment it also 'pings' on my laptop. I really can't understate how useful the widget and cross-platform integration is, because for someone like me who procrastinates a lot and forgets what I'm meant to be doing at any random moment, it's so useful to just open up my phone and instantly have my most important tasks/habits slap me in the face, demanding my attention. This also ties in nicely with the way notifications/alerts work. I've got reminders set on all my habits, and when the reminders go off, they actually "take over" the entire screen, at which point I can tick them off, or dig into the more extensive options on the back-end. There's a few areas I can see for quality-of-life improvements, though I'm optimistic that their subscription model means we haven't seen the "final" iteration of this app for some time yet. A few things that jump out at me over a couple months' usage: -- To mark a habit as "incomplete", you can't just double-tap the checkbox for an 'X' mark, you have to open the app, pull up the relevant habit in the dashboard, go into its settings, and the option is buried all the way in the app's back-end menus. It's a minor gripe, but when compounded over weeks or months of use, it's easy to just not bother marking your "failures" at all. It makes me wonder if there's other useful features I've missed just because they're not readily accessible on the front end UI + widgets. -- It would be nice if habits displayed in the widget + front-end UI had a visual indicator of how many days that habit has been on "streak" for. You can track those metrics, but again it's hidden in the robust-yet-opaque back-end, accessible via sub-menus and abstract graphs, rather than being loudly displayed front-and-centre. I'd probably be more motivated to "keep the streak going" with a given habit if I could see at a split-second glance how today's efforts fit into the context of the previous 7 days, or whatever. --Also, you can set habits to only repeat on certain days of the week, or a certain number of times per week, but again its not really visible at a quick glance to know if you're on track or falling behind. By which I mean, when I pull up my habits for Thursdayy, for instance, and I see "exercise at gym" in my list of habits for that day, then surely I should get some indication of "you've been to the gym X times this week so far, and you have Y gym sessions remaining for this week [in order to fulfil your habitual obligations]". Again, the information is there in the app, but you have to actively seek it out. Maybe the more fastidious time-keepers will see to this without batting an eye, but for forgetful, ADHD-prone types like myself, if it's not right in front of me then it might as well not exist. But all in all, these are minor foibles. Fantastic app. 5/5.
